newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Police stop 80,000 marchers, skirmishes erupt.
newsitem.headline: Police stop 80,000 marchers, skirmishes erupt.

text.p: Scores of angry youths hurled stones at Serbian riot police on Monday hours after more than 100 pro-democracy protesters were injured in the bloodiest street battles seen in Belgrade for years.

When pieces of paving stones rained down, police pursued the youths, some of whom took refuge in a department store. According to B92 independent radio, police cornered and beat some of them, arresting several.
Tension rose earlier on Monday afternoon when anti-riot police halted 80,000 opposition protesters in downtown Belgrade in a new confrontation only hours after the overnight clashes.

Western governments swiftly condemned the autocratic Serbian President Slobodan imposition of international sanctions against Serbiseen a was unlikely. At first police did not react to the stone-throwing, witnesses said, but simply used their long anti-riot shields to protect themslves against about 200 stone-throwers witnesses described as young militants.

Witnesses said police in body armour, helmets and carrying riot shields, drew their U.S.-style truncheons, but the protestors' own stewards formed a cordon to keep the whistling, shouting opposition marchers away from police lines.

Two hours earlier police had allowed more than 20,000 student protestors o march over a Belgrade river bridge after having halted and then attacked opposition activists in the same spot on Sunday night.

More than 100 people were hurt in Sunday night's street battles in the city's old quarter with police repeatedly charging and clubbing demonstrators, some of whom fought back by hurling bottles, bricks and stones.

Opposition demonstrators regrouped on Monday and rallied without hindrance in Republic Square but ran quickly into a phalanx of police when they tried to march down a main boulevard, the witnesses said.

About 500 police stood several deep across the avenue. The police commander told one of the opposition leaders, Zoran Djindjic, he would not let them pass but would not resort to force without provocation, a Reuters news team said.
The protest organisers set up a 100-metre (300-foot) gap between marchers and police. Djindjic asked the protesters to disperse to avoid bloodshed.
Most of them did so, but several dozen youths ranged up and down the street, hurling stones and rubbish at police.
They ignored opposition leaders' calls to use passive resistance in the face of police attacks.

"Let us fight last night's brutal crime with smiles and songs", opposition politician Vuk Draskovic told supporters. "...this is only the beginning of our Gandhi-style protest, not its end. We shall take on violence with non-violence."

Milosevic unleashed his police on the opposition coalition, Zajedno, with the clock ticking towards legal deadlines this week for rulings on opposiion appeals against the annulment of local election losses in Belgrade and other towns by his ruling Socialist Party.

Djindjic, co-leader of the oppisition coalition, also urged demonstrators who have been rallying daily on the streets for three months, not to be provoked into violence to avoid giving Milosevic a pretext for emergency rule.
Serbian churchmen and soldiers have joined opposition demands for recognition of the November 17 election results.
Orthodox Church Patriarch Pavle lashed out at Milosevic's government on Monday, saying it was "tragically...sinking more and more into ignorance of what it is doing."
